Photograph: Darren England/AAP Housing House prices slide across Australia as Middle East conflict and tax changes begin to bite Cotality data shows a drop in Brisbane, Adelaide and Perth, as nation’s median home price falls about $19,000 below its March peak Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Luca Ittimani Sun 2 Aug 2026 10.01 EDT Last modified on Sun 2 Aug 2026 10.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google House prices have fallen in Brisbane, Adelaide and Perth as the market downturn spreads across Australia. New Cotality data, released on Monday, showed prices have fallen across most of the nation since May. Brisbane’s median price has fallen about $8,000 since May, to equal its March level of $1.1m. The city’s dwelling prices had increased for an historic 40 consecutive months, since February 2023, until they fell in June. Fines, indefinite motel stays and uncertainty: how a homeless camp exposed regional Australia’s housing crisis Read more Adelaide and Perth median home prices have each fallen about $4,000 below their record highs set in May, at $944,000 and $1.03m respectively. In June, regional Australia’s home values fell overall for the first time since January 2023. Regional home values fell or stayed flat in every state in July. Nationally, the median home price is now $928,000 – about $19,000 below its March peak. Sydney, Melbourne and Canberra median prices have respectively fallen $69,000, $39,000 and $22,000 since February. Prices in Sydney and Melbourne are still higher than they were in January 2025 and in Canberra are above where they were in September 2025. Prices are still higher than January 2025 The Reserve Bank has reported fewer than 1% of borrowers have fallen into negative equity, with home values worth less than their loans, while an even smaller share are unable to make repayments. The housing market has slowed since February, when the Reserve Bank of Australia began to hike interest rates and the US war on Iran broke out. Housing demand has fallen further since the May federal budget trimmed property investors’ tax concessions. Capital gains tax changes are already having an impact on wealth inequality – and vested interests are running scared | Greg Jericho Read more NAB on Thursday reported a 15% fall in home loan applications from the first three months of 2026 to the three months to June. Westpac, Equifax and Loan Market have independently reported falling mortgage demand. The RBA governor, Michele Bullock, speaking at an Anika Foundation lunch on Wednesday, said she was surprised by the slump in house prices and housing demand since May. Bullock said interest rates were only “a bit” restrictive, attributing the slump to falling buyer demand. “I expect that things will settle down,” Bullock said. “People will get used to the new rules. Hopefully the conflict overseas will die down, and they’ll get a bit more confidence. Prices might lower a bit. People might feel more confident to come back into the market.” Buyers and sellers are already showing signs of adjustment, with auction clearance rates edging up from from their June low of 47.4% to reach 53.6% at the weekend, according to Cotality’s preliminary data. The property research company reported the number of new listings had declined over July as sellers held off going to market to wait out weak conditions. The RBA is not expected to raise interest rates when its board next meets on 11 August. Market Mastery Webinar by Vishal Malkan Find the weak links in your portfolio by Vishal Malkan Register for FREE Webinar Register for FREE Estonian Defence Minister Hanno Pevkur has resigned following a controversy over a €70 million ammunition procurement meant to support Ukraine, after a government supplier failed to deliver the expected artillery shells on schedule. Pevkur, who has headed Estonia’s defence ministry since 2022, said he was stepping down to accept political responsibility for shortcomings in the defence sector, even as he maintained that he was not personally involved in negotiating individual contracts. “Estonian security is not a one-man project. It is our joint responsibility. That is why I must take political responsibility for the entire defence field today,” Pevkur said in a social media post. The procurement involved Datasel SRL, an Italy-based company acquired by India’s Neco Defence Munitions in 2024. Estonia’s Centre for Defence Investments (RKIK) entered into several contracts with the company to secure artillery ammunition for Ukraine, which was facing shortages of shells during its war with Russia. The deal was financed through the European Union’s European Peace Facility, with Estonia making substantial advance payments. According to Estonia’s public broadcaster ERR and reports by Eesti Ekspress and Postimees , the payments eventually totalled about €70 million. Estonia began contracting Datasel in August 2024, initially paying roughly €15 million upfront. Another agreement followed in October, with additional contracts subsequently taking the advance payments to around €70 million by the end of the year, according to the reports. The ammunition was supposed to be supplied within months. Deliveries were, however, repeatedly delayed amid reported production difficulties. When ammunition was eventually received in 2025, it did not meet the required quality standards, Eesti Ekspress reported. Datasel had no previous record of producing or selling artillery shells and that the ammunition received was not ultimately sent to Ukraine, it has been further learnt from a report by The Telegraph . Following this, RKIK terminated the contracts and sought the return of the advance payments. Estonia has taken the dispute to international arbitration as it attempts to recover the money. The supplier, however, has rejected Estonia's account of the matter. Datasel has argued that it delivered a substantial quantity of munitions and disputed the claims that quality problems justified termination of the contracts. According to Eesti Ekspress , the company said it had supplied goods and submitted invoices worth approximately €58 million. Datasel also confirmed receiving around €59 million in advance payments. “Datasel is the party that has suffered losses in connection with these supply contracts,” the company said through its lawyer, according to the newspaper. It further claimed that the reasons cited by Estonia for terminating the agreements were “contradictory and illogical”. Datasel acknowledged delays but disputed claims that the ammunition supplied was unusable. The company said it was prepared to complete the contracts if RKIK fulfilled its own obligations. The dispute has now become a legal battle, with Estonia seeking to recover the funds and Datasel challenging the termination of its contracts. Elmar Vaher, director general of RKIK, said the contract should not have been awarded to the company in the first place. “In my opinion, we should not have signed a contract with them,” Vaher told Eesti Ekspress . He compared the decision to hiring an inexperienced builder. “If I start building a house and hire a company that has never built houses before, there is a doubt that the house will not be finished,” Vaher said. Pevkur's resignation came as Estonia's National Audit Office scrutinised the country's defence spending and procurement practices. An audit released on August 28 identified problems relating to the management of defence funds and the accounting of military assets, according to ERR . The watchdog warned that Estonia could be forced to bear the €70 million cost from its own budget if the money cannot be recovered from the disputed procurement. The matter has also attracted the attention of the European Commission because the ammunition purchase was financed with EU money. Commission spokesperson Christian Wigand said the bloc had safeguards and recovery mechanisms intended to protect EU funds. Pevkur defended the existing division of responsibilities, arguing that ministers do not personally conduct individual procurement negotiations. “The defence minister does not conduct contract negotiations; the defence minister does not count socks and ammunition. The defence minister makes the fundamental decision to support Ukraine,” he said, according to ERR. He also said he had not read the contracts, pointing out that detailed procurement work was handled by RKIK. The minister faced further scrutiny in parliament on Wednesday, where lawmakers questioned him about the procurement controversy. Pevkur described the matter as an “ordinary contract dispute”, while stressing the exceptional pressure on European countries to secure ammunition for Ukraine during a period of global shortages. Estonia's defence procurement agency has previously promoted itself as a fast-moving buyer capable of helping other European countries secure weapons for Ukraine. Pevkur said the agency had executed roughly €400 million in contracts on behalf of international donors. Despite his resignation, Pevkur maintained that Estonia had made the right strategic choices to strengthen its security. “Estonia is better protected than ever before,” he wrote.
